rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> 2-year split-plot field experiment in Corvallis, OR with three irrigation systems x three ETc levels, five replicates. Q2: Table 4 and Abstract <U+2013> Phytophthora cinnamomi root infection averaged 14.3% with drip vs 6.7<U+2013>7.3% with sprinklers and microsprays; drip plants had half the shoot and root dry weight and lower root vigor; Discussion <U+2013> drip likely increased root rot because it maintained higher soil water content near plant base. Q4: Table 2 and Fig. 1 <U+2013> soil water content in top 0.3 m measured by TDR was 5<U+2013>6% higher under drip in 2005 and soil was often saturated (>30%) under drip at 100<U+2013>150% ETc; Fig. 4B <U+2013> root vigor linearly related to Phytophthora infection (70% of variation). Q7: Results/Summary <U+2013> infection increased with amount of water applied (Fig. 3), and authors state the effect occurs where soil is saturated/over-applied and at sites with heavy soil, poor drainage or disease history; study site itself was silty clay loam. Q8: Discussion <U+2013> authors note 'Duke' is highly susceptible and could become infected from inoculum below the detection limit of their soil and well-water tests; source of inoculum could not be determined; further study needed on drip lateral placement/frequency.
rows.notes: Q3 answered no: root rot was established by root plating on selective media (one method); visual symptoms, root-vigor ratings and dry weights are growth/indirect indicators rather than an independent disease measurement, so treated as not triangulated. Q9: tables report means with letter groupings and P-values only; no SD/SE/CI stated in text (error bars in figures not visible in this text). Q7 and Q8 are moderate yeses: the condition of over-application/saturation and heavy soil is drawn partly from own data (silty clay loam, saturation at 100<U+2013>150% ETc) and partly from literature; the limitation statement concerns cultivar susceptibility and undetected inoculum.

notes: Full text appears complete. Single site, single cultivar ('Duke'), one soil type (Malabon silty clay loam), two seasons, plot scale. The study directly supports the claim that drip maintains higher soil moisture near the plant base and increases Phytophthora root rot in highbush blueberry.
